title: Competition and Consumer Amendment (Strengthening Rules About Misuse of Market Power) Bill 2013

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would broaden misuse of market power rules to cover likely harm to competition across markets and the supply chains serving them.
It would give the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission investigation powers, including requiring documents, answers and a published statement about supply chain impacts.
The expanded test would cover conduct reasonably likely to damage competitors, prevent market entry or lessen competition, including effects beyond the market where conduct occurs.
changes: The Commission could require a corporation to prepare a supply chain impact statement.
False or misleading responses to Commission investigations would be prohibited.
Most information supplied to the Commission would be protected, while supply chain impact statements would require publication.
summary.affected: Corporations with substantial market power, participants in affected supply chains and the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission are affected.

speeches.speaker: Robert Oakeshott
speeches.brief: Presented a bill to strengthen competition and consumer laws by extending consideration of broader market impacts and future consequences, allowing the ACCC to compel relevant supply-chain documents and requiring supply chain impact statements from businesses seeking greater market power. Argued that these measures could address supermarket bargaining imbalances while supporting farmers, suppliers and consumers.

speeches.speaker: Bernie Ripoll
speeches.brief: Moved that private members' business on the Competition and Consumer Amendment (Strengthening Rules About Misuse of Market Power) Bill 2013 and on cyber-safety be referred to the Federation Chamber for further consideration.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Argued that competition laws had encouraged excessive market concentration and harmed consumers, citing supermarket prices, supplier rebates and a two-litre Coke price rising from $2.97 to $3.95 over five years, and supported a coalition root-and-branch review.
